options.a: 2 inches (5 cm) on the center of the chest
options.b: 2.4 inches (6 cm) on the upper third of the breastbone
options.c: 3 inches (7.5 cm) on the center of the chest
options.d: Two inches over the xiphoid at the lower tip of the breastbone

distractorExplanations.b: 2.4 inches (6 cm) is the upper depth limit, not the minimum, and the hands belong on the lower half of the sternum, not the upper third.
distractorExplanations.c: 3 inches exceeds the recommended 2.4-inch (6 cm) maximum for adults; compressing that deep raises the risk of chest injury.
distractorExplanations.d: Right depth, wrong spot: pressing on the xiphoid tip can injure the liver; hands go on the lower half of the sternum, center of the chest.

options.a: Finish five cycles of CPR before you attach the pads
options.b: Check the pulse for 30 seconds before using it
options.c: Attach the pads over the shirt to save time
options.d: Turn it on and follow the prompts; bare the chest

distractorExplanations.a: Delaying the AED for set CPR cycles is outdated; the AED is turned on and attached as soon as it arrives, with CPR continuing until pads are on.
distractorExplanations.b: Pulse checks are limited to 10 seconds and lay rescuers skip them; an unresponsive non-breathing person gets the AED without delay.
distractorExplanations.c: AED pads must contact bare, dry skin; clothing blocks the electrode contact and can cause burns or a failed shock.

options.a: Resume CPR immediately
options.b: Do a pulse check
options.c: Use the recovery position
options.d: Wait for the AED to reanalyze

distractorExplanations.b: A no-shock advisory is not a sign of a pulse; rescuers resume compressions right away rather than pausing to check for a pulse.
distractorExplanations.c: The recovery position is for a person who is breathing normally; a no-shock message during arrest still means continued CPR.
distractorExplanations.d: The AED reanalyzes after about 2 minutes of CPR; waiting idle for that analysis leaves the brain without any circulation.

options.a: Abdominal thrusts to drain water from the lungs before starting any CPR
options.b: CPR starting with compressions (and breaths as trained) after a safe remove
options.c: Rescue breaths only, because drowning is a breathing problem
options.d: CPR without an AED, since a wet chest makes defibrillation unsafe

distractorExplanations.a: Draining water with abdominal thrusts is not recommended; it delays ventilation and compressions and raises vomiting and aspiration risk.
distractorExplanations.c: Breaths alone do not circulate blood; a drowning victim without normal breathing needs full CPR with compressions plus breaths.
distractorExplanations.d: The AED is still used for drowning: move the person out of standing water, dry the chest, and attach the pads.

options.a: The heel of both hands stacked, as for an adult
options.b: Two fingers placed just below the breastbone tip
options.c: Two fingers or two thumbs encircling, as trained
options.d: One thumb pressing to a depth of about 2 inches

distractorExplanations.a: The two-hand stacked adult technique is too forceful and too wide for an infant chest and risks injury to the ribs and organs.
distractorExplanations.b: Fingers go on the sternum just below the nipple line; pressing below the breastbone tip lands on the xiphoid and abdomen.
distractorExplanations.d: Infant depth is about 1.5 inches (4 cm), one-third of chest depth; 2 inches is the adult and child target, and one thumb is not a taught method.

first-aid-cpr-readiness-check-cpr-007.explanation: Infants are not small adults. This item asks: “Infant compressions use:”. The matching answer is: Two fingers or two thumbs encircling, as trained — not adult full palms on the gut. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official first-aid / CPR paper. Do not use adult full palms on the gut.

options.a: Replace chest compressions with breaths
options.b: Measure the patient's exhaled air
options.c: Give oxygen without ventilating
options.d: Give breaths with less exposure

distractorExplanations.a: A barrier device makes breaths safer but does not replace compressions; circulation still depends on high-quality chest compressions.
distractorExplanations.b: A pocket mask or bag-mask has no measuring function; measuring exhaled CO2 is done with capnography by advanced providers.
distractorExplanations.c: A mask is used to deliver breaths; oxygen with no ventilation does not move air in and out of a non-breathing patient.

options.a: 2 minutes or when the AED analyzes
options.b: 5 minutes, or sooner if the rescuer asks
options.c: 10 minutes or when the rescuer feels tired
options.d: Every 30 compressions during each breath pause

distractorExplanations.b: Five minutes is too long; compression depth and rate decline within about 2 minutes, often before the rescuer notices fatigue.
distractorExplanations.c: Rescuers do not reliably feel fatigue until quality has already dropped; switching on a 2-minute schedule prevents shallow compressions.
distractorExplanations.d: Switching every cycle adds handoff pauses about every 18 seconds; rescuers switch every 5 cycles, about 2 minutes.

first-aid-cpr-readiness-check-cpr-009.explanation: Fatigue wrecks depth. This item asks: “Switch compressors about every:”. The matching answer is: 2 minutes or when the AED analyzes, to fight fatigue. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official first-aid / CPR paper. Switching that often fights fatigue.

options.a: Turning the AED to pediatric mode to lower the energy
options.b: Moving to a reasonably dry area and drying the chest
options.c: Placing the pads on the back instead of the chest
options.d: Waiting until paramedics arrive with a manual defibrillator

distractorExplanations.a: Pediatric mode is for children under 8 or about 55 lb; lowering energy does not address the conduction hazard of standing water.
distractorExplanations.c: Moving the pads to the back does not solve the water problem; the patient must be moved out of the puddle and the chest dried.
distractorExplanations.d: Delaying defibrillation lowers survival; lay rescuers can safely use the AED once the person is out of standing water with a dry chest.

options.a: Use the recovery position and monitor
options.b: Give two breaths, then recheck
options.c: Start CPR — that is not normal breathing
options.d: The patient is breathing, so CPR is not needed

distractorExplanations.a: The recovery position is for normal breathing with a pulse; agonal gasping signals cardiac arrest, which needs CPR.
distractorExplanations.b: Lay rescuer CPR starts with compressions; giving breaths and pausing to recheck delays circulation for a patient in arrest.
distractorExplanations.d: Agonal gasps are not effective breathing; they occur in the first minutes of cardiac arrest and are a cue to start CPR.

options.a: Place pads at least an inch away; do not put a pad on a medicine patch
options.b: Place a pad directly over the device so the shock reaches the heart
options.c: Skip the AED, since an implanted device will deliver its own shock
options.d: Leave the medicine patch in place and put the pad right over it

distractorExplanations.b: A pad over an implanted device can damage it and block energy delivery; pads are offset from the device bulge.
distractorExplanations.c: A pacemaker does not defibrillate, and even a patient with an ICD still gets an AED if arrest continues.
distractorExplanations.d: A medication patch under a pad blocks energy transfer and can burn; remove the patch with a gloved hand and wipe the skin.

options.a: CPR with the patient tilted onto her right side to take weight off the uterus
options.b: CPR with a left uterine displacement as trained — do not skip compressions
options.c: Withhold the AED to protect the fetus until obstetrics arrives
options.d: Compressions placed lower, on the abdomen just above the uterus

distractorExplanations.a: Aortocaval relief uses left uterine displacement; tilting to the right keeps the uterus on the vena cava and reduces blood return.
distractorExplanations.c: The AED is used as usual in pregnancy; maternal defibrillation is the best chance for both mother and fetus.
distractorExplanations.d: Hand position stays on the lower half of the sternum; compressing the abdomen is ineffective and can injure the uterus.

options.a: Twenty minutes have passed without a pulse, even if help has not arrived
options.b: The AED gives a no-shock message, showing the heart cannot be restarted
options.c: A trained team takes over, an obvious fatal injury, or you are too exhausted
options.d: A bystander says the person has a DNR, though no document is shown

distractorExplanations.a: Lay rescuers do not stop on a timer; termination decisions belong to EMS and medical direction, not a fixed 20-minute rule.
distractorExplanations.b: A no-shock message means the rhythm is not shockable, not that care is futile; rescuers resume CPR immediately.
distractorExplanations.d: A valid DNR order stops CPR, but an unverified verbal claim from a bystander does not; continue until a document or EMS directs otherwise.

first-aid-cpr-readiness-check-cpr-015.explanation: Have a reason. This item asks: “You stop CPR when:”. The matching answer is: A trained team takes over, an obvious fatal injury, or you are too exhausted and no one can continue. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official first-aid / CPR paper. Stop if you are too exhausted and no one can continue.

options.a: Elevating the limb above the heart and pressing on a pressure point
options.b: A loose tourniquet so blood still reaches the hand
options.c: Removing soaked dressings and replacing them with clean ones
options.d: Direct pressure, then a tourniquet if trained and needed

distractorExplanations.a: Elevation and pressure points are no longer recommended for severe bleeding; firm direct pressure and a tourniquet are.
distractorExplanations.b: A loose tourniquet blocks venous return but not arterial flow, which increases bleeding; it must be tight enough to stop the bleeding.
distractorExplanations.c: Removing soaked dressings tears away forming clot; add more dressing on top and keep pressing.

options.a: High on the limb, not over a joint
options.b: Directly over the knee or elbow
options.c: Just below the wound, closer to the hand
options.d: On the limb, loosened every 15 minutes

distractorExplanations.b: A joint prevents the strap from compressing the artery; the tourniquet goes on the limb above the joint, not over it.
distractorExplanations.c: A tourniquet must sit between the wound and the heart; placing it distal to the wound does not stop the arterial flow feeding it.
distractorExplanations.d: Periodic loosening is outdated and restarts bleeding; once applied, the tourniquet stays tight until hospital care.

first-aid-cpr-readiness-check-bleeding-0.explanation: Tight and timed. This item asks: “A tourniquet goes:”. The matching answer is: High on the limb, not over a joint, and is not loosened as a game. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official first-aid / CPR paper. Once applied it is not loosened.

options.a: Flushed, hot, dry skin with a slow, bounding pulse
options.b: Pale and sweaty — give water freely and raise the head
options.c: Pale, sweaty, anxious, weak pulse — keep warm and get ALS
options.d: Slow pulse and calm mood — cool them to slow the bleeding

distractorExplanations.a: That pattern fits heat illness, not hemorrhagic shock; blood loss causes pale, cool, clammy skin with a rapid, weak pulse.
distractorExplanations.b: Oral fluids are withheld in shock (aspiration and possible surgery), and the person is kept lying flat, not sitting up.
distractorExplanations.d: Shock brings a fast pulse and anxiety, and cooling worsens it; the person is kept warm while EMS is on the way.

options.a: Removed at once so direct pressure can be applied to the wound
options.b: Cut flush with the skin, then covered with a tight dressing
options.c: Twisted gently to check depth before bandaging around it
options.d: Stabilized, not pulled in the field unless it blocks the airway

distractorExplanations.a: Pulling the object out can release the tamponade it provides and start heavy bleeding; it is stabilized in place.
distractorExplanations.b: Cutting it at skin level removes the grip needed to stabilize it and a tight dressing drives it deeper; pad around it instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Any manipulation of an impaled object can cut vessels and tissue; it is padded and stabilized without probing depth.

options.a: Wrapped, bagged dry then on ice — not in water
options.b: Packed directly in ice so it stays as cold as possible
options.c: Placed in a cup of tap water to keep it moist
options.d: Wrapped in gauze and kept warm in a pocket

distractorExplanations.b: Direct contact with ice freezes the tissue and ruins replantation; the bagged part is placed on ice, not in it.
distractorExplanations.c: Soaking in water waterlogs and damages the tissue; the part is wrapped, sealed in a dry bag, then cooled.
distractorExplanations.d: Warmth speeds tissue death; the part needs to be kept cool (bag on ice) to stay viable for replantation.

first-aid-cpr-readiness-check-bleeding-0.explanation: Replant starts with the part. This item asks: “A severed finger is:”. The matching answer is: Wrapped, bagged dry then on ice — not in water, go with the patient. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official first-aid / CPR paper. Send it with the patient.

options.a: Heavy bleeding from the mouth as the only reliable sign
options.b: Pain, rigidity, or shock with little external blood
options.c: Bruising alone, which means it can wait until tomorrow
options.d: A slow, strong pulse and warm, flushed skin

distractorExplanations.a: Internal bleeding often shows no visible blood at all; pain, abdominal rigidity, and shock signs are the clues.
distractorExplanations.c: Bruising can appear late and does not measure blood loss; any shock signs after a crash need 911 now.
distractorExplanations.d: That is the opposite of blood loss; internal hemorrhage produces a rapid, weak pulse and pale, cool skin.

options.a: Optional with family
options.b: Needed only for large wounds
options.c: Standard
options.d: For EMS

distractorExplanations.a: Family members can still carry bloodborne pathogens; gloves are standard precautions for any blood contact, known person or not.
distractorExplanations.b: Bloodborne exposure risk does not depend on wound size; gloves are standard for any contact with blood.
distractorExplanations.d: Gloves are not reserved for professional responders; any first aider touching blood uses them as a standard precaution.

options.a: Gets firm pressure even over a skull dent
options.b: Is left uncovered so the wound can drain
options.c: Is usually minor, so skip direct pressure
options.d: Still gets pressure — scalps bleed a lot

distractorExplanations.a: Over a suspected depressed skull fracture, firm pressure can push bone fragments inward; press gently around the edges instead.
distractorExplanations.b: Leaving a heavy scalp bleed open lets blood loss continue; it needs a dressing and direct pressure.
distractorExplanations.c: Scalp wounds bleed heavily because of rich blood supply; they still need pressure and can hide head trauma.

first-aid-cpr-readiness-check-bleeding-0.explanation: Scalp ≠ always minor. This item asks: “A scalp bleed that looks huge:”. The matching answer is: Still gets pressure — scalps bleed a lot; watch the neck/c-spine if the mechanism is trauma. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official first-aid / CPR paper. Watch the neck/c-spine if the mechanism is trauma.

options.a: Seal as trained (occlusive) and get ALS
options.b: Pack the hole tightly with gauze and press
options.c: Give rescue breaths to reinflate the lung
options.d: Pour saline in the wound to clean it first

distractorExplanations.b: Wound packing is for junctional or limb bleeding, not an open chest wound; packing the chest can worsen breathing.
distractorExplanations.c: A breathing patient does not get rescue breaths; a collapsed lung from a chest wound needs advanced care, not ventilation by a bystander.
distractorExplanations.d: Irrigating an open chest wound delays care and can introduce fluid into the chest cavity; cleaning is for minor wounds.

first-aid-cpr-readiness-check-bleeding-0.explanation: Sucking chest wounds are ALS. This item asks: “A puncture to the chest that bubbles:”. The matching answer is: Seal as trained (occlusive) and get ALS — this is not a band-aid job. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official first-aid / CPR paper. This is not a band-aid job.

options.a: The patient's blood pressure
options.b: The time it went on
options.c: The time you plan to loosen it
options.d: The wound's size

distractorExplanations.a: First aiders have no way to measure blood pressure reliably; the application time is what guides limb-ischemia decisions.
distractorExplanations.c: Tourniquets are not scheduled for loosening in the field; only the time it went on is recorded for the hospital.
distractorExplanations.d: Wound size does not tell the hospital how long the limb has been without blood flow; the application time does.

options.a: Tilt the head back and pinch the bridge of the nose
options.b: Pack tissue deep into the nostril and have them lie down
options.c: Pinch and calm — do not have them lie flat swallowing blood
options.d: Pinch for 30 seconds, then let go to check if it stopped

distractorExplanations.a: Tilting the head back makes the child swallow blood, and the bony bridge is the wrong spot; pinch the soft part and lean forward.
distractorExplanations.b: Deep packing can injure the nose and lying down sends blood down the throat; sit up, lean forward, and pinch.
distractorExplanations.d: Thirty seconds is far too short; continuous pressure for about 10 minutes is needed before checking.

options.a: Search the area right away, then think about scene safety
options.b: Call 911 and leave, since there is no patient to treat
options.c: Clean up the blood first so no one else slips in it
options.d: Scene safety first, then search/call — do not slip in it

distractorExplanations.a: Sequence error: scene safety is checked first, before searching, so the rescuer does not become a second victim.
distractorExplanations.b: A pool of blood signals a likely injured person nearby; after securing the scene you call and search for them.
distractorExplanations.c: Cleaning blood without PPE is an exposure risk and delays finding the injured person; scene check, call, then search.

options.a: Faster escalation — pressure still first
options.b: A tourniquet first instead of direct pressure
options.c: Aspirin or ibuprofen for the pain
options.d: Lighter pressure to avoid bruising

distractorExplanations.b: A bleeding disorder does not skip direct pressure; a tourniquet is for life-threatening limb bleeding that pressure fails to control.
distractorExplanations.c: Aspirin and NSAIDs impair platelet function and worsen bleeding, especially in a patient with a clotting disorder.
distractorExplanations.d: These patients need firm, longer pressure, not lighter pressure; bruising risk is secondary to controlling the bleed.

options.a: Scrub it out with a stiff brush before bandaging
options.b: Do not carve it out; control bleed and get care
options.c: Dig it out with tweezers so it does not tattoo
options.d: Seal it in with skin glue to stop the bleeding

distractorExplanations.a: Aggressive scrubbing tears more tissue; first aid is gentle irrigation, bleeding control, and clinical removal of embedded grit.
distractorExplanations.c: Digging out embedded gravel in the field causes damage and infection; a clinician removes it with anesthesia.
distractorExplanations.d: Gluing over embedded debris traps contamination and causes infection; the wound needs cleaning by a clinician.

options.a: Any hives, even with normal breathing
options.b: Asthma attacks when the inhaler is empty
options.c: Anaphylaxis — inject as trained and call 911
options.d: Low blood sugar in a known diabetic

distractorExplanations.a: Skin-only hives without breathing or circulation signs are not anaphylaxis; epinephrine is for multi-system or airway involvement.
distractorExplanations.b: The auto-injector treats anaphylaxis; an asthma attack without an allergic trigger needs the inhaler and 911, not someone's EpiPen.
distractorExplanations.d: Hypoglycemia is treated with oral sugar if able to swallow or glucagon; epinephrine is not a glucose treatment.

options.a: Give a dose of their insulin to steady them
options.b: Give a sugar-free drink to avoid a spike
options.c: Give a protein bar and wait an hour
options.d: Give fast sugar if they can swallow safely

distractorExplanations.a: Insulin lowers blood sugar further; shaky and sweaty in a diabetic suggests hypoglycemia, which needs sugar.
distractorExplanations.b: Diet drinks contain no glucose; low blood sugar needs about 15–20 g of fast sugar such as juice or glucose tablets.
distractorExplanations.c: Protein and fat slow absorption; give fast sugar first and recheck in about 15 minutes, not an hour.

options.a: Let them rest and recheck the signs in an hour
options.b: Note the time and get emergency care
options.c: Give aspirin right away, as for a heart attack
options.d: Drive them to their usual clinic tomorrow

distractorExplanations.a: Time is brain: clot-busting treatment has a narrow window, so waiting an hour to recheck loses treatable time.
distractorExplanations.c: A stroke may be a bleed; aspirin is a heart-attack measure and is not given in first aid for suspected stroke.
distractorExplanations.d: Suspected stroke needs 911 and a stroke-capable hospital now; waiting for a routine clinic visit tomorrow loses the treatment window.

first-aid-cpr-readiness-check-medical-03.explanation: Time is brain. This item asks: “Stroke signs (FAST) mean:”. The matching answer is: Note the time and get emergency care — do not give them a full meal to 'test'. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official first-aid / CPR paper. Do not give them a full meal to 'test'.

options.a: Have them walk around to see if the pain eases with movement
options.b: Give nitroglycerin from a friend's prescription to test it
options.c: Have them rest, 911, aspirin if your protocol and they can swallow
options.d: Drive them to the hospital yourself to save time over 911

distractorExplanations.a: Exertion increases the heart's oxygen demand; possible cardiac chest pain calls for rest, not a walking test.
distractorExplanations.b: Only the patient's own prescribed nitroglycerin is assisted; someone else's dose can drop blood pressure dangerously.
distractorExplanations.d: EMS starts treatment and an ECG on scene and can manage an arrest en route; a private car cannot.

options.a: Gets something placed between the teeth to stop tongue biting
options.b: Needs the limbs held down firmly to stop the jerking
options.c: Can be watched until it ends, then call 911 if needed
options.d: Is status — 911, protect the head, nothing in the mouth

distractorExplanations.a: Objects in the mouth break teeth and block the airway; nothing goes in the mouth of a seizing person.
distractorExplanations.b: Restraining a seizing person causes fractures and soft-tissue injury; clear the area and protect the head instead.
distractorExplanations.c: A seizure past 5 minutes is status epilepticus; 911 is called at the 5-minute mark, not after it ends.

options.a: Help with their own inhaler as trained and get ALS if they are tiring
options.b: Have them breathe into a paper bag to slow their breathing
options.c: Lay them flat to rest and hold off on the inhaler until EMS arrives
options.d: Give an antihistamine tablet and wait for it to work

distractorExplanations.b: Paper-bag rebreathing is a hyperventilation myth; in asthma it worsens low oxygen and delays the inhaler.
distractorExplanations.c: A person in respiratory distress sits upright, and the prescribed inhaler is used now, not held for EMS.
distractorExplanations.d: Antihistamines do not open constricted airways; severe asthma needs the bronchodilator inhaler and EMS.

options.a: Sit them upright on a chair so they can recover
options.b: Lower them, legs up if no trauma, check breathing
options.c: Use smelling salts to wake them before checking breathing
options.d: Give them water to drink while they are still drowsy

distractorExplanations.a: Keeping a fainting person upright reduces blood flow to the brain and risks another faint and a fall; lay them down.
distractorExplanations.c: Smelling salts are not recommended and delay the airway and breathing check, which comes first.
distractorExplanations.d: A drowsy person may not protect the airway; nothing by mouth until fully alert and able to swallow.

options.a: A local reaction that only needs ice
options.b: A mild allergy treated with an antihistamine
options.c: Anaphylaxis until proven otherwise
options.d: An asthma attack unrelated to the sting

distractorExplanations.a: Hives plus wheeze involve skin and airway, two body systems; that is anaphylaxis, not a local reaction treated with ice.
distractorExplanations.b: Antihistamines do not reverse airway swelling; wheeze after a sting needs epinephrine and 911.
distractorExplanations.d: New wheeze with hives right after a sting points to anaphylaxis; calling it asthma delays epinephrine.

options.a: Flat on their back with the head raised
options.b: Black coffee to sober them up quickly
options.c: A cold shower to bring them around
options.d: Recovery position if they have a pulse

distractorExplanations.a: Lying on the back lets vomit run into the airway; the side-lying recovery position lets it drain out.
distractorExplanations.b: Caffeine does not reverse intoxication and adds to vomiting risk; airway protection is the priority.
distractorExplanations.c: A cold shower risks hypothermia and falls and does nothing to protect the airway from vomit.

first-aid-cpr-readiness-check-medical-04.explanation: Aspiration kills. This item asks: “Someone drunk and vomiting:”. The matching answer is: Recovery position if they have a pulse and you cannot protect the airway sitting. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official first-aid / CPR paper. Use it when you cannot protect the airway with them sitting.

options.a: Do not pour juice in the mouth — 911 and glucagon if trained
options.b: Rub honey inside the cheek and wait 15 minutes before calling 911
options.c: Give their insulin injection since they are diabetic
options.d: Sit them up and give sips of a sugary drink

distractorExplanations.b: Putting food in an unresponsive person's mouth risks aspiration, and waiting to call 911 delays definitive care.
distractorExplanations.c: Insulin drives blood sugar even lower; an unresponsive hypoglycemic person needs glucagon or EMS glucose.
distractorExplanations.d: An unresponsive person cannot swallow safely; oral sugar is only for someone awake who can swallow.

options.a: Have them breathe into a paper bag until they calm down
options.b: Treat the ABCs you see and get help if breathing is failing
options.c: Tell them to calm down, since it is likely just panic
options.d: Wait to call for help until you know which one it is

distractorExplanations.a: Paper-bag rebreathing can drop oxygen levels and is dangerous if the cause is actually asthma.
distractorExplanations.c: Assuming panic can miss a real asthma attack; first aiders treat what they see and get help if breathing fails.
distractorExplanations.d: First aiders do not need a diagnosis to act; delaying help while sorting panic from asthma risks respiratory failure.

options.a: Shade, fluids, and rest first
options.b: Salt tablets and a cool drink
options.c: Aggressive cooling and 911
options.d: Fever reducers like acetaminophen

distractorExplanations.a: Shade, fluids, and rest are heat-exhaustion care; heat stroke with altered mental status needs immediate rapid cooling.
distractorExplanations.b: Salt tablets are not recommended and an altered person may aspirate; heat stroke needs whole-body cooling and EMS.
distractorExplanations.d: Antipyretics do not work in heat stroke, which is not a fever; they can also stress an injured liver.

first-aid-cpr-readiness-check-medical-04.explanation: CNS change = emergency. This item asks: “Heat stroke (hot, altered) needs:”. The matching answer is: Aggressive cooling and 911 — not just a sip of water on a bench. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official first-aid / CPR paper. Not just a sip of water on a bench.

options.a: Syrup of ipecac to make the child vomit
options.b: Milk or water to dilute it before calling
options.c: Activated charcoal from the home medicine cabinet
options.d: Poison control / 911 — do not invent an emetic

distractorExplanations.a: Ipecac is no longer recommended; induced vomiting can cause aspiration and further injury from caustic substances.
distractorExplanations.b: Routine dilution is not recommended and delays expert advice; call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) or 911 first.
distractorExplanations.c: Activated charcoal is given only on Poison Control or medical instruction, not routinely by a first aider.

options.a: Cognitive practice — not an AHA course card
options.b: An official AHA BLS Provider written exam form
options.c: A Red Cross certificate once you score 84%
options.d: An OSHA-accepted first aid certification

distractorExplanations.b: This is an independent UniPrep diagnostic; the BLS written exam is given only inside an AHA course.
distractorExplanations.c: Red Cross certification requires its own course and skills check; scoring on an online mock earns no certificate.
distractorExplanations.d: OSHA-accepted first aid training includes hands-on skills practice; an online knowledge mock does not certify anyone.

options.a: Straightened gently before splinting to restore alignment
options.b: Splinted in the position found if you are trained, pulse checked
options.c: Splinted tightly, with circulation checked once EMS arrives
options.d: Left alone if the person can still move the fingers

distractorExplanations.a: Realignment is a trained EMS step for a pulseless limb; first aiders splint a suspected fracture in the position found.
distractorExplanations.c: Circulation, sensation, and movement are checked before and after splinting, and a splint that is too tight cuts off blood flow.
distractorExplanations.d: Finger movement does not rule out a fracture; a painful, deformed forearm is splinted as a suspected break.

options.a: Sit them up slowly to check whether they can move their neck
options.b: Place a pillow under the head for comfort and wait
options.c: Manual stabilization, 911 — do not sit them up to 'see'
options.d: Have them walk to the car if they can feel their legs

distractorExplanations.a: Moving the head to test it can turn an unstable fracture into a cord injury; hold the head still until EMS arrives.
distractorExplanations.b: A pillow flexes the neck out of line; manual stabilization keeps the head in a neutral position.
distractorExplanations.d: Normal sensation does not rule out an unstable spinal fracture; a diving injury stays still with manual stabilization.

options.a: Apply ice packs directly to cool the burn fast
options.b: Cover with butter or ointment, then call 911
options.c: Pop the blisters and cover with a tight bandage
options.d: Cool with water, cover, 911 — no toothpaste

distractorExplanations.a: Ice causes cold injury to burned tissue and hypothermia over a large area; cool running water is used instead.
distractorExplanations.b: Butter and greasy ointments trap heat and raise infection risk; cool with water and cover with a clean dressing.
distractorExplanations.c: Blisters protect against infection and should be left intact; burns get a loose, clean covering.

options.a: Long rinse and emergency care
options.b: A neutralizing solution, then a rinse
options.c: A brief rinse and an eye patch
options.d: Rubbing the eye clear

distractorExplanations.b: Neutralizing a chemical in the eye can cause a heat reaction and delays flushing; plain water irrigation comes first.
distractorExplanations.c: A brief rinse leaves chemical on the eye; irrigation continues for at least 15–20 minutes before transport.
distractorExplanations.d: Rubbing grinds the chemical into the cornea and adds abrasion; the eye is flushed with running water.

options.a: Rubbed with snow to restore blood flow
options.b: Rewarmed gently; do not rub snow on it
options.c: Thawed near a fire or heater
options.d: Rewarmed in the field even if it may refreeze

distractorExplanations.a: Rubbing frozen tissue, with or without snow, causes mechanical damage to ice-crystal-filled cells; rewarm gently.
distractorExplanations.c: Numb frostbitten tissue cannot sense heat and burns easily; rewarm in warm (not hot) water instead of dry heat.
distractorExplanations.d: Thaw-refreeze cycles cause more damage than staying frozen; rewarm only when refreezing can be prevented.

options.a: Heat right away to loosen it
options.b: Ice applied directly to the skin for an hour
options.c: Rest, ice, compression, elevation
options.d: Walking on it to keep the joint loose

distractorExplanations.a: Heat on a fresh sprain or strain increases swelling; the first 24–48 hours call for cold, not heat.
distractorExplanations.b: Ice goes on for about 20 minutes with a cloth barrier; an hour on bare skin risks cold injury.
distractorExplanations.d: Loading a fresh sprain worsens the injury; rest comes first, and inability to bear weight needs medical care.

first-aid-cpr-readiness-check-injury-051.explanation: RICE/POLICE variants. This item asks: “A sprain vs strain in first aid is treated with:”. The matching answer is: Rest, ice, compression, elevation as appropriate — still get care if they cannot bear weight. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official first-aid / CPR paper. Still get care if they cannot bear weight.

options.a: Pick it up by the root and scrub it clean under the tap
options.b: Wrap it in a dry tissue until you reach the dentist
options.c: Store it in a glass of tap water until the dentist can see you
options.d: Pick it up by the crown, keep it moist, see a dentist fast

distractorExplanations.a: Handling or scrubbing the root destroys the periodontal ligament cells needed for reimplantation; hold the crown only.
distractorExplanations.b: Drying kills periodontal ligament cells within minutes; keep the tooth moist in milk, saline, or a tooth-storage solution.
distractorExplanations.c: Tap water is hypotonic and damages root cells; milk, saline, or a tooth-preservation solution is used instead.

first-aid-cpr-readiness-check-injury-052.explanation: Time and the periodontal ligament. This item asks: “A tooth knocked out:”. The matching answer is: Pick it up by the crown, keep it moist as trained, see a dentist fast. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official first-aid / CPR paper. Keep it moist as trained.

options.a: Cover, control bleed, do not push bone back
options.b: Push the bone back in, then bandage it
options.c: Rinse the bone end and leave it uncovered
options.d: Tourniquet it routinely, even with minor bleeding

distractorExplanations.b: Pushing the bone back drags contamination deep into the wound; cover it and stabilize the limb as found.
distractorExplanations.c: An open fracture is covered with a sterile dressing to limit infection; leaving it exposed increases contamination.
distractorExplanations.d: A tourniquet is for life-threatening limb bleeding only; routine use for minor bleeding risks limb ischemia.

options.a: Hold a hot match to it so it backs out on its own
options.b: Pull straight with tweezers; save the tick if told
options.c: Twist and jerk quickly so the head comes out with it
options.d: Smother it in petroleum jelly and wait for it to detach

distractorExplanations.a: CDC advises against heat; burning the tick can make it release more fluid into the bite and burns the skin.
distractorExplanations.c: Twisting or jerking breaks off the mouthparts in the skin; use steady, even upward pressure.
distractorExplanations.d: Smothering with jelly is a folk remedy that delays removal; prompt removal with tweezers lowers infection risk.

first-aid-cpr-readiness-check-injury-054.explanation: Straight pull. This item asks: “A tick found attached:”. The matching answer is: Pull straight with tweezers as public-health guidance says; save the tick if told. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official first-aid / CPR paper. Follow public-health guidance.

options.a: A shot of alcohol to warm them from inside
options.b: A hot bath right away to rewarm fast
options.c: Dry, insulate, warm drinks if they can swallow
options.d: Rub the arms and legs hard to boost circulation

distractorExplanations.a: Alcohol dilates skin vessels and increases heat loss; it worsens hypothermia despite the warm feeling.
distractorExplanations.b: Rapid immersion rewarming can cause afterdrop and burns; mild hypothermia is rewarmed gradually with dry insulation.
distractorExplanations.d: Vigorous rubbing can push cold blood to the core and cause afterdrop; handle gently and insulate instead.

options.a: Soak in hydrogen peroxide, then seal it with a bandage
options.b: Wash and bandage; tetanus only matters for deep cuts
options.c: Squeeze it to bleed out the rust, then leave it open
options.d: Wash, cover, and urgent care for tetanus status

distractorExplanations.a: Peroxide damages healthy tissue and does not address tetanus; wash with soap and water and check tetanus status.
distractorExplanations.b: Puncture wounds are classic tetanus-prone wounds because they are deep and low-oxygen; vaccination status must be checked.
distractorExplanations.c: Rust is not the tetanus risk and squeezing does not remove spores; wash, cover, and get tetanus status reviewed.

first-aid-cpr-readiness-check-injury-056.explanation: Tetanus is a shot question. This item asks: “A puncture from a rusty nail:”. The matching answer is: Wash, cover, and urgent care for tetanus status — do not ignore. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official first-aid / CPR paper. Do not ignore it.

options.a: Treat as a partial amp — do not complete it
options.b: Cut the skin bridge and bag the part on ice
options.c: Let it hang freely so you can see the bleeding
options.d: Pack the gap with ice to slow the bleeding

distractorExplanations.b: Completing a partial amputation destroys remaining vessels and nerves that may support reattachment; leave the bridge intact.
distractorExplanations.c: A hanging part twists the skin bridge and its vessels; support the part in normal position with a bulky dressing.
distractorExplanations.d: Direct ice on exposed tissue causes cold injury; bleeding is controlled with direct pressure and dressings.

options.a: Yank it straight back out the way it went in
options.b: Leave it and get care unless you are trained
options.c: Push it through, then pull it back out
options.d: Cut the shank flush with the skin

distractorExplanations.a: Pulling a buried barb backward tears tissue; it is left in place unless a trained removal method is used.
distractorExplanations.c: Pushing the barb through without cutting it off and then backing it out tears tissue twice; the trained method cuts the barb.
distractorExplanations.d: Cutting the shank flush leaves the hook buried with nothing to grip, making clinical removal harder.

first-aid-cpr-readiness-check-injury-058.explanation: Barbs catch. This item asks: “A fishhook in a finger with the barb buried:”. The matching answer is: Leave it and get care unless you are trained on the advance-and-cut method. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official first-aid / CPR paper. Trained rescuers may use the advance-and-cut method.

options.a: Victims carry a charge, so wait before touching them
options.b: Shelter under a tall, isolated tree with the victims
options.c: The storm can still hit — move to safer ground
options.d: Treat the moving, groaning victims before silent ones

distractorExplanations.a: Lightning victims do not retain an electrical charge; they can be touched and treated right away.
distractorExplanations.b: Tall isolated objects attract strikes and side flashes; a tree is one of the most dangerous places in a storm.
distractorExplanations.d: Lightning uses reverse triage: the silent, pulseless victims are treated first because the others are usually breathing.

first-aid-cpr-readiness-check-injury-059.explanation: Reverse triage is a lightning oddity. This item asks: “Lightning scene safety means:”. The matching answer is: The storm can still hit — move to safer ground after the immediate reverse-triage of the pulseless. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official first-aid / CPR paper. Immediate reverse-triage of the pulseless comes before moving.

options.a: Call 911 and describe the signs you are seeing
options.b: Wear gloves and use a pocket-mask barrier for any rescue breaths
options.c: Ask an alert adult for consent before helping
options.d: Invent a diagnosis or withhold 911 to 'not embarrass them'

distractorExplanations.a: Calling 911 and reporting observed signs is core first aid, well within a lay responder's role.
distractorExplanations.b: Gloves and a barrier device are standard precautions for first aiders, not clinical overreach.
distractorExplanations.c: Getting consent from a responsive adult is a required first-aid step, not acting as a clinician.
